edges.justification: Book‑to‑market ratio is calculated at the start of the year; lower BTM values are associated with higher expected future returns, influencing the 12‑month stock return.
Unexpected earnings during the year lead to price adjustments that directly affect the stock’s total return over the same period.
The month in which a firm’s fiscal year ends determines the timing of earnings releases and market reactions, which can shape the 12‑month return.
A firm’s performance over the year influences institutional investors’ decisions to buy or sell shares in the following year.
Leverage measured at the start reflects a firm’s risk profile; higher leverage can impact risk‑adjusted returns.
Market‑wide returns drive individual stock returns through beta exposure.
Momentum from historical performance often predicts future returns, influencing the annual return.
Value index membership, based on book‑to‑market, is empirically linked to expected return patterns.
Lower BTM suggests undervaluation, which can lead to larger earnings surprises when earnings exceed forecasts.
Fiscal year end timing influences the book value used to compute BTM at the start of the year.
Lower BTM attracts institutional investors, leading to higher ownership changes.
Historical returns influence market valuation at the start of the year, affecting BTM.
Value index membership is directly determined by the book‑to‑market ratio at the start of the year.
Fiscal year end month affects the timing of earnings releases and can influence the magnitude of earnings surprises.
Significant earnings surprises prompt institutional investors to adjust their holdings.
High leverage can constrain earnings growth, making earnings more likely to differ from analysts’ forecasts.
Past performance shapes analysts’ forecasts, affecting the size of the earnings surprise.
Unexpected earnings improve the profitability component of the end‑of‑year quality score.
The timing of the fiscal year end influences when institutional investors rebalance, affecting ownership changes.
Fiscal year end month affects debt reporting and therefore the leverage ratio at the start of the next year.
Fiscal year end timing can impact profitability and safety metrics that constitute the quality score.
Fiscal year end month influences the book‑to‑market calculation, affecting index membership.
Firms with higher leverage are perceived as riskier, prompting institutional investors to reduce holdings.
Market performance influences institutional portfolio allocation decisions, altering ownership levels.
Historical performance attracts institutional investors, leading to higher ownership changes.
Higher quality firms attract institutional ownership in the following year.
Value index membership signals undervaluation, drawing institutional investors.
Leverage contributes to the safety component of the quality score.
Historical returns reflect sustainable profitability, influencing the end‑of‑year quality score.

AnnualReturn is measured over the twelve months following the start of the year, whereas QualityScore is computed at the end of that same year from firm fundamentals. Therefore the return influences the quality score, not vice versa. The correct direction is AnnualReturn → QualityScore.
